for the first four years of the depression we raised each year one-third of the amount required to relieve unemployment. It was a three-way payment plan; one-third was raised by private subscription; one-third came from the province and one-third from the federal government. During those four years not one cent of the money required to take care of the unemployed was charged against municipal taxes. To-day what do we find? We are able to reduce our mill rate without increasing assessments.
I want to commend the earnest endeavour of the Minister of Labour to relieve this situation. I speak particularly of the housing plan and the home improvement plan; they have taken up a great deal of the slack in our district. I do not know of any year for the last eight or ten in which we had as much home building as during the past year. And that can be enlarged. As we all know, there is no line of industrial endeavour which gives as much employment to labour as building. I am told by contractors that if you trace a building back to its elements, eighty-three per cent of the cost goes for labour. So that anything done to enlarge the building program would assist materially in lightening the burden of unemployment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: FEDERAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIRECT RELIEF- CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM AFFECTING SOCIAL SERVICES
speechtext: About eighty-five per cent is labour in the home improvement plan.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIRECT RELIEF- CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM AFFECTING SOCIAL SERVICES
speechtext:
And about eighty-three per cent in new housing.
Another matter of which I want to speak for a moment is the plan on which these funds are distributed. I do not want to say anything derogatory to municipal control. Perhaps it is all right; I have no knowledge. But if I may be allowed a personal word, in Galt we appointed a committee of patriotic citizens who handled our unemployment relief funds during the four years of which I have spoken. They did this very satisfactorily. Careful attention was given to all cases; they were carefully investigated and relief was paid in a satisfactory way where required. In distributing relief through the province and down through the municipality, without implying anything, I think there is a temptation there, and with some people the temptation to play municipal politics is very strong. So that if relief can be handled, particularly where large amounts are involved, by an independent committee at the final distribution of the funds, that I think is very desirable indeed.
Now, to get back to the resolution, we all know it is nearly impossible for the municipalities to carry this burden of relief. The taxation on real estate to-day is so heavy

that building houses for rental or investment is almost prohibitive. No one can get even a modest return on the investment. There is plenty of money for this sort of investment if only people were assured of even a modest return. Under these circumstances the burden of unemployment relief appears to be a national burden. It should come back in its entirety to the federal government. I hope the municipalities will cooperate to the extent of reducing their requirements to the minimum by handling relief funds very carefully.
I am going to offer a suggestion to the Minister of Labour as to how this relief problem could be handled. I do not mean distribution. My idea is this, that interference in private business over a period of years has been greatly responsible for the situation we are in to-day. For the past twenty years Anglo-Saxon America has been playing the game of government in business. Whether it has been wheat marketing, railways, mortgaging or whatever else you wish, when private enterprise got into any difficulty whatever the solution was to put the government in. Well, we have had an opportuni'y to see just how that has worked over quite a period of years. That has been a commonplace, as I say, for a long time. That is what happened in Canada in connection with radio. After five years of experimenting with radio I do not think I would be amiss in saying that conditions are in a rather bad state. I was going to say they were in a sorry' mess, but I would hardly go that far. Instead of achieving the goal of Canadianizing the air, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation coast to coast network, built at considerable cost to the Canadian taxpayer, is now being used as a cut-rate pipe line to give much prized supplementary facilities to American broadcasters in the Canadian market.
The point I wish to make is that the only way to take up the slack is to encourage private industry, to stop continually sniping at successful private business, and to aid business in every legitimate way possible. I feel sure that if this is done, the heavy fog of unemployment and unrest will rapidly pass away. I was going to speak last night, but did not have an opportunity to do so. I find to-day however, that I am in very distinguished company in what I have said. According to this morning's Gazette, Sir Josiah Stamp, speaking in New York last night, said something very much along the same line, and I should like to read just two or three extracts from his remarks. He was addressing the British Empire Chamber of

Unemployment Relief-Federal Responsibility
Commerce in New York city and went on to state what were the key factors of the economic outlook, outlining four points bearing on the recession, which he described as "convenient to watch". Three of the points were mechanical and the other psychological. The first mechanical point was that of credit and monetary facilities. The second mechanical factor was the effect of taxation, and I suspect that the effect of the undistributed profits tax appeared there. I want to say here that another very great load on industry to-day is the heavy sales tax we have in this country, which of course has to be taken up by the consumer. The third mechanical factor was the industrial question, and he believed that the best prosperity was secured by allowing business to make good profits. This may seem terrible to some members of the house, but this is what he said:
The higher profits are, the more rapid expansion and employment .	.	. but if costs,
particularly wage levels and hours of working, are forcibly thrown out of relation with prices the margin of profit is in jeopardy, and restriction of production is inevitable.
Then he went on to discuss the psychological feature of it, and said:
My fourth factor is psychological. So long as business is afraid of what the government will do it can make no long distance plan for development and political fears are the worst enemies of economic progress.
If I have any suggestion to offer to the government to-day, it is this: I am not going to say that the government snipes at business, but we have a good many people who continually snipe at business not only in the house but on the platforms throughout the country. It is a popular thing to do, and it is a very easy thing to do. But private business, under proper supervision, is the right idea for handling this unemployment situation, and I do not think there is the least doubt but that given a chance it will gradually work us out of that difficulty. Just to give an idea of the different businesses that have been socialized-I am not going to say anything about that at the present moment, but I might say-

speechtext: I should say it is not greater than in 1933, but greater than what the government was paying in the latter part of 1934. Certainly that would be so after August, 1934, when the old system of the dominion government paying thirty-three and a third per cent of the total cost was superseded by the present system of grants in aid. For example, the dominion contribution in November, 1935 to the province of Ontario represented twenty per cent of the total cost of relief in that province. We are paying much more now than we did in 1934 and in most of 1935.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIRECT RELIEF- CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM AFFECTING SOCIAL SERVICES
speechtext: I want to find out if the proportion now borne by the municipalities is greater than it was in 1934.

speechtext: It is really not possible to answer that question, as I have not those figures here. My hon. friend is also aware that the percentage borne by the municipalities varies not only within the provinces but as between the provinces.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIRECT RELIEF- CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM AFFECTING SOCIAL SERVICES
speechtext: How do they arrive at the amount of the grants in aid? Is that worked out on a percentage basis in connection with each province?

subsubtopic: FEDERAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIRECT RELIEF- CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM AFFECTING SOCIAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The amount is based upon an estimate of what will be required for the forthcoming year. A lump sum is allocated by this parliament to the various provinces on the basis of those unemployed, qualified by the financial position of the province. It is not possible to reduce that to the terms of an algebraic formula, but looking back over the years I believe we would be justified in saying that the allocation among the provinces has been fair and reasonable, having regard to the problem itself and the financial position of the several provinces.
If we did not have recourse to the income tax to raise the money required by the dominion government taking over the entire

cost of relief, we would have to consider the sales tax. I think it will be agreed that here again we would be burdening that group of moderate wage earners who represent, so to speak, the working force of the country as a whole. Not only that, but with an increase in the sales tax we would be providing another deterrent to a revival of the building industry.
I do not propose to develop these points any further. I have brought them out simply as an illustration of the difficulties that would confront the dominion government in assuming the entire financial responsibility for relief within the present structure of the constitution. I use those words deliberately because it has been agreed generally, both by the preceding administration and the present government, that so far as present constitutional responsibility is concerned, the primary responsibility lies with the municipalities, while the responsibility in a secondary sense lies with the provincial governments. The dominion government goes in to assist the province when the problem has reached the point where it is beyond provincial resources. I do not suggest that an improvised method of dealing with the situation has been wholly satisfactory. We are doing our utmost to improve it from time to time, and the agreements now before the provinces are designed for that purpose. I believe that when these agreements are fully understood and accepted by the provinces, we shall be able to remove some, at any rate, of the abuses which now exist in the administration of relief.
But there is also another reason why it would be most unwise for the dominion government at this time, as suggested in this resolution, to assume the entire responsibility for relief. That reason lies in the fact that the relief problem at present is not wholly an unemployment problem. Relief lists in all provinces have been heavily charged with charity cases and unemployables. That, I am quite sure, is within the knowledge of any member of the house who has had close acquaintance with the development of relief during recent years. It is clear, therefore, that as the relief problem is contracted, this constant element of unemployables becomes relatively greater in the total. It is greater to-day than it was a year ago. It was greater then than it was the year before that. So this proposal means in effect that the dominion government at this time is asked not only to take over unemployment relief but also to take over from the provinces the care of unemployables. Now, if the dominion government had not already accepted some

But, as it has already been pointed out this afternoon. the dominion government, through old age pensions, through pensions for the blind, through special care for unemployed pensioners, through provision which is now in contemplation for an extension of allowances to unemployed war veterans, has already taken over from the provinces a very considerable part of the burden of unemployable persons. That being the case, I certainly feel it would be a great mistake for the dominion, in advance of a further review and readjustment. of its relations wi-tih the provinces, to assume this new burden and to do so, as proposed here, "notwithstanding the provisions of any law, statute, usage or custom to the contrary."
There is a further reason why this proposal would not be satisfactory at this time.

speechtext:
I wish to refer finally to
the reason why the dominion government should not at this time under existing conditions assume entire responsibility for relief. I refer to the question of administration. This resolution does not make any reference to administration, but I would like hon. members to realize that under present conditions the administration of relief is conducted almost exclusively by officials of our municipal governments. They have gained a very wide experience in these last years, and many of them administer relief without additional recompense of any kind. If the dominion government assumed responsibility for relief, it is clear, I think, that this would mean of necessity the setting up of a self-perpetuating organization for administration and at the present time there is no branch of the government that is equipped with an organization suitable to deal with relief across the entire dominion. The one organization which would be useful in this connection is the employment service of Canada, but that employment service is not a national employment service in the strict sense of the word. Contributions are made to it by the dominion government, but the actual control of it lies with the provinces.
Not only that, but if the mover of the resolution does not suggest that the dominion should take over the cost of administration of relief and does mean that the dominion should pay the entire cost but leave the administration to the municipalities, it is clear that we shall be entering into a most vicious arrangement. Under that arrangement municipalities, instead of having two or three dollars from outside to one of their own to expend, would receive all that was required for relief purposes without at the same time being responsible in any way for raising that money by taxation. I believe we have had sufficient experience in this country with the abuses of a system of that kind to convince us that, whatever the errors of the past may have been, we certainly ought not to repeat and extend them at this time.
Finally, as to the proposal for constitutional reform, it does seem to me that my hon. friend who has suggested in the first part of his resolution that the dominion government should take over the entire cost of relief has, so to speak, allowed the horse to be stolen
Questions

and in the second part of the resolution is professing a willingness to lock the stable door. I feel there is a grave necessity for a constitutional revision and this whole question of relief and social service must play an important part in that investigation, but certainly, in advance of that investigation, it would be folly for the dominion government to assume this entire burden of unemployment relief, without any readjustment of powers or revenues of the provinces.
